nodes.title: Custom domain support?
nodes.body:
Hi, 
dou you have any plans for custom domains?

- CNAME on my domain to the <id>.opentunnel.xyz
- `opentunnel route add 3000 --domain mynas.example.com`
- optionally pin the certificate in my DNS, so it will mitigate MITM by your infra

Currently I do such thing on $2 VPS (nginx -> Tailscale -> NAS), but I prefer to pay it to you, so I don't need to manage the VPS.

not today, tunnels only get `<route>.<id>.opentunnel.xyz` names. it fits how things work though: tls already ends on your machine, so the server would just need to route a verified hostname (cname plus a txt record to prove you own it) to your tunnel, and the client would get the cert for it. a CAA record pinned to your own acme account would cover the mitm part. checking with the team whether we

Btw, I see market for this feature in the NAS users, especially in Home Assistant community. Theere are some easy to use solutions, but none has this privacy benefit - TLS termination on the NAS and IP hidden from the clients.

I would write addon for the Home Assistant OS for this.

nodes.title: Server: support DNS-01 providers other than Cloudflare (Route 53, or a generic hook)
nodes.body:
### Summary

DNS-01 challenges only work against Cloudflare: `DNS_PROVIDER` is `cloudflare` or `challtestsrv`. Every tunnel gets a wildcard certificate, so DNS-01 is mandatory, and a self-hosted `opentunnel-server` needs its tunnel domain on Cloudflare. For a deployment in AWS with the zone in Route 53, that means moving or delegating the zone to Cloudflare only for challenge records.

I understan

makes sense. the hook provider looks like the cleaner option to me since it covers every provider. self-hosting the server isn't something we've really supported so far, so i want to check with the team before adding to it. leaving this open for now.

— from 𝕺𝖕𝖊𝖓𝕮𝖔𝖉𝖊

went with the hook. it's on master (36ffded): set `DNS_PROVIDER=exec` and `DNS_HOOK=/path/to/hook`, and the server runs `<hook> create <name> <value>` / `<hook> delete <name> <value>` with no shell. exit 0 means success; on failure the error includes the exit status and the end of stderr.

nodes.title: SDK: read the API URL from `OPENTUNNEL_API` when `api` is not passed
nodes.body:
### Summary

The TypeScript SDK only talks to a server other than `https://opentunnel.xyz` when the app passes `api` to `OpenTunnelClient.layer()`. Apps that embed the SDK usually don't expose that, so their users can't point them at a self-hosted server. The CLI already reads `OPENTUNNEL_API` (the hidden `--api` flag); the SDK has no equivalent.

nodes.title: UDP routes: forward local UDP services (games, WireGuard, DNS) over the tunnel
nodes.body:
## Proposal

Support UDP services alongside TLS routes:

```bash
opentunnel route add 27015 --udp
# Added route 5f1c0e2a9b7d4e36 → 127.0.0.1:27015 (udp)
# udp://<id>.opentunnel.xyz:40123
```

UDP has no SNI to route by, so each UDP route gets a public UDP port of its own, and its datagrams are carried over the existing bridge WebSocket. I know the project doesn't take pull requests, so here is a c

Thanks for the detailed proposal and for working out a full reference implementation. It answers most of the questions we'd have asked.

UDP routes would be a real change in what OpenTunnel is. Today every route is TLS that ends on your own machine and is routed by hostname. UDP needs dedicated public ports, a port allocator, a new kind of frame on the bridge, and routes that aren't end-to-end enc

An update from the maintainers: we're not sure about UDP. The core promise of OpenTunnel is that traffic stays end-to-end encrypted, with TLS ending on your own machine and our servers only ever passing ciphertext. UDP routes couldn't keep that promise, since there's no TLS to terminate, so they'd only be as private as whatever protocol runs inside them. That makes it feel like a different product

nodes.title: TypeScript SDK bridge WebSocket ignores HTTP(S)_PROXY / ALL_PROXY (breaks opencode remote access behind a proxy)
nodes.body:
### Summary

The TypeScript SDK's bridge WebSocket does not honor proxy environment variables. In the same process, `fetch()` goes through the proxy, so tunnel creation and certificate issuance succeed; the `wss://opentunnel.xyz/api/tunnel/<id>/connect` bridge then dials the origin directly. On an egress-controlled network the bridge never attaches and the tunnel is unusable.
